title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 870–873 (Night 205, continuing nights-204), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 205 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The Lady Budūr opens the letter, finds her own ring in it, and knows that the astrologer behind the curtain is her beloved; beside herself with joy she recites four lines on tears of gladness, then braces her feet against the wall, breaks the iron collar from her neck and the chains, and runs out to kiss and embrace him. The eunuch fetches King al-Ghayūr, and Budūr, covering her head before her father, recites two punning lines on the tooth-stick, siwāk, and the arāk tree. Overjoyed at her recovery, the king hears Qamar al-Zamān's lineage and the whole story of the exchanged rings, says it deserves to be written in the chronicles, and has the marriage contract drawn up at once; the city is decorated, the wedding is held, and the two spend their first night together, followed by a month of feasting for the people of the Inner and Outer Islands. After a while Qamar al-Zamān's father, King Shahramān, appears to him in a dream reproaching him in two lines of verse; he wakes troubled, tells Budūr what he saw, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and fifth night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the fifth after the two hundred”: al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا وَضَعَ الْخَاتَمَ فِى الْوَرَقَةِ وَنَاوَلَهَا لِلْخَادِمِ فَأَخَذَهَا وَدَخَلَ بِهَا إِلَى السِّتِّ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā waḍaʿa al-khātama fī al-waraqati wa-nāwalahā li-al-khādimi fa-akhadhahā wa-dakhala bihā ilā al-sitti Budūra
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-put the-ring in the-sheet and-handed-it to-the-eunuch, he (the eunuch)-took-it and-went-in with-it to the-Lady Budūr,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān had put the ring in the letter and handed it to the eunuch, the eunuch took it and went in with it to the Lady Budūr;
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together, السعيدان; it is kept as set. Shahrazād takes up the story at the point where the last night broke off. lammā, “when”, opens a clause whose answer is fa-akhadhahā, “he took it”: the eunuch. nāwala, Form III, “to hand”, with li- marking the one handed to. dakhala bi-, “to go in with”, bi- marking what is carried; ilā marks the person he goes to. The print spells fī as فى, with ى, as it often does.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهَا مِنْ يَدِ الْخَادِمِ وَفَتَحَتْهَا فَوَجَدَتْ خَاتَمَهَا فِيهَا بِعَيْنِهِ فَقَرَأَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathā min yadi al-khādimi wa-fataḥathā fa-wajadat khātamahā fīhā bi-ʿaynihi fa-qaraʾati al-waraqata
sentences.l: and-she-took-it from (the) hand (of) the-eunuch and-opened-it, and-found her-ring in-it, itself, and-read the-sheet.
sentences.i: and she took it from the eunuch's hand, opened it, and found in it her own ring, the very one; and she read the letter.
sentences.n: bi-ʿaynihi, “with its eye”, that is “itself, the very same”: ʿayn, “eye, essence”, with bi- in the idiom of identity, and -hi returning to the ring. The hamza of فقرأت is printed; the kasra on its tāʾ only links it to the article that follows.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَرَفَتِ الْمَقْصُودَ عَلِمَتْ أَنَّهُ مَعْشُوقُهَا وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ الْوَاقِفُ خَلْفَ السِّتَارَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿarafati al-maqṣūda ʿalimat annahu maʿshūquhā wa-annahu huwa al-wāqifu khalfa al-sitārati
sentences.l: And-when she-knew the-intended(-meaning), she-knew that-he (was) her-beloved and-that-he, he (was) the-one-standing behind the-curtain.
sentences.i: When she understood what it meant, she knew that he was her beloved, and that he was the one standing behind the curtain.
sentences.n: al-maqṣūd, “what is intended”, passive participle of qaṣada: the meaning of the letter. maʿshūq, “beloved”, passive participle of ʿashiqa, “to love passionately”. annahu huwa al-wāqifu, “that he, he is the one standing”: the pronoun huwa repeats the subject to single him out.

sentences.t: فَطَارَ عَقْلُهَا مِنَ الْفَرَحِ وَانْشَرَحَ صَدْرُهَا وَاتَّسَعَ وَمِنْ فَرْطِ الْمَسَرَّاتِ أَنْشَدَتْ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭāra ʿaqluhā mina al-faraḥi wa-insharaḥa ṣadruhā wa-ittasaʿa wa-min farṭi al-masarrāti anshadat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-flew her-mind from the-joy, and-opened her-breast and-widened; and-from (the) excess (of) the-delights she-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Her wits flew from her for joy, her heart opened and grew wide, and out of the fullness of her delight she recited these verses:
sentences.n: ṭāra ʿaqluhā, “her mind flew”, a common way of saying one is beside oneself. insharaḥa ṣadruhā, “her breast expanded”, Form VII of sharaḥa: the Arabic picture of gladness, as constriction of the breast is of grief; ittasaʿa, Form VIII of wasiʿa, “to grow wide”, repeats it. min marks the cause twice, mina al-faraḥi and min farṭi. farṭ, “excess”; masarrāt, “joys”, plural of masarra.

sentences.t:
وَلَقَدْ نَدِمْتُ عَلَى تَفَرُّقِ شَمْلنَا * نَدَمًا وَفَاضَ الدَّمْعُ مِنْ اَجْفَانِيْ
وَنَذَرْتُ اِنْ عَادَ الزَّمَانُ يَلُمُّنَا * مَا عُدْتُ اَذْكُرُ فُرْقَةً بِلِسَانِيْ
هَجَمَ السُّرُوْرُ عَلَيَّ حَتَّى انَّهُ * مِنْ عَظْمِ مَا قَدْ سَرَّنِيْ اَبْكَانِيْ
يَاعَيْنُ صَارَ الدَّمْعُ مِنْكَ سَجِيَّةً * تَبْكِيْنَ مِنْ فَرَحٍ وَمِنْ اَحْزَانِيْ
sentences.tr:
wa-laqad nadimtu ʿalā tafarruqi shamlinā * nadaman wa-fāḍa al-damʿu min ajfānī
wa-nadhartu in ʿāda al-zamānu yalummunā * mā ʿudtu adhkuru furqatan bi-lisānī
hajama al-surūru ʿalayya ḥattā innahu * min ʿaẓmi mā qad sarranī abkānī
yā ʿaynu ṣāra al-damʿu minka sajiyyatan * tabkīna min faraḥin wa-min aḥzānī
sentences.l:
And-indeed I-regretted over (the) scattering (of) our-union * (with) a-regret, and-overflowed the-tear from my-eyelids;
and-I-vowed (that) if returned the-time gathering-us, * not would-I-again mention parting with-my-tongue.
Rushed the-joy upon-me, until indeed-it, * from (the) greatness (of) what had gladdened-me, made-me-weep.
O eye, has-become the-tear from-you a-habit: * you-weep from joy and-from my-sorrows.
sentences.i:
I grieved over the breaking-up of our union * with such grief that tears flooded from my eyes,
and vowed that if time should bring us together again, * never again would my tongue so much as speak of parting.
Joy has rushed upon me, so that, * for the very greatness of my gladness, it makes me weep.
O eye, tears have become your nature: * you weep for joy and for my sorrows alike.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on ajfānī / lisānī / abkānī / aḥzānī. nadimtu ʿalā, “I regretted”, ʿalā marking what is regretted; nadaman, the verbal noun as an inner object, gives emphasis. shaml, “union, the gathering of friends”; tafarruq shamlinā, “the scattering of our union”, a set phrase, and its opposite, jamʿ shamlinā, comes in the prose just after. nadhartu in …, “I vowed that if …”: lamma, “to gather”, in yalummunā, “gathering us”, a circumstantial imperfect. mā ʿudtu adhkuru, “I would not again mention”: ʿāda with an imperfect means “to do again”. ḥattā innahu, “so much that it …”: the print leaves the alif of انَّهُ without its kasra and hamza. The print points عَظْمِ, ʿaẓm, “bone”; the sense wants ʿuẓm, “greatness”, the same letters with the closed first syllable the metre needs (ʿiẓam would not scan); the print's pointing is kept. abkānī, Form IV of bakā, “it made me weep”. The print runs yā and ʿaynu together, يَاعَيْنُ; ʿayn, “eye”, is feminine and so is tabkīna, “you weep”, but the print points minka, masculine; both are kept. sajiyya, “natural disposition, habit”. The print sets a sukūn on several long vowels, as it often does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا قَامَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَصَلَبَتْ رِجْلَيْهَا فِى الْحَائِطِ وَاتَّكَأَتْ بِقُوَّتِهَا عَلَى الْغُلِّ الْحَدِيدِ فَقَطَعَتْهُ مِنْ رَقَبَتِهَا وَقَطَعَتِ السَّلَاسِلَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghati al-sittu Budūru min shiʿrihā qāmat min waqtihā wa-ṣalabat rijlayhā fī al-ḥāʾiṭi wa-ittakaʾat bi-quwwatihā ʿalā al-ghulli al-ḥadīdi fa-qaṭaʿathu min raqabatihā wa-qaṭaʿati al-salāsila
sentences.l: And-when finished the-Lady Budūr from her-verse, she-rose from her-time, and-braced her-two-legs in the-wall, and-leaned with-her-strength on the-collar the-iron, and-broke-it from her-neck, and-broke the-chains.
sentences.i: When the Lady Budūr had finished her verses she rose at once, braced her feet against the wall, threw all her strength against the iron collar, and broke it from her neck, and broke the chains.
sentences.n: The print has فرعت, a misprint for فرغت, corrected here. faragha min, “to finish”, min marking what is finished. min waqtihā, “from her time”, that is “at once”. ṣalaba, here in its later sense “to set firm, brace” (in Classical Arabic Form I means “to crucify”): she sets her feet hard against the wall; fī here is “against”. Budūr has been kept chained as a madwoman. ittakaʾa ʿalā, Form VIII, “to lean, bear down on”, with bi-quwwatihā, “with her strength”, bi- marking the means; the hamza of واتّكأت and its shadda are printed. ghull, “iron collar, shackle for the neck”, and al-ḥadīd, “iron”, set beside it as a description, “the collar, the iron one”; its shadda is printed. salāsil, plural of silsila, “chain”. The ئ of الحائط is printed.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ خَلْفِ السِّتَارَةِ وَرَمَتْ نَفْسَهَا عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَبَّلَتْهُ فِي فَمِهِ مِثْلَ زَقِّ الْحَمَامِ وَعَانَقَتْهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ مَابِهَا مِنَ الْوَجْدِ وَالْغَرَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-kharajat min khalfi al-sitārati wa-ramat nafsahā ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-qabbalathu fī famihi mithla zaqqi al-ḥamāmi wa-ʿānaqathu min shiddati mā bihā mina al-wajdi wa-al-gharāmi
sentences.l: And-she-came-out from behind the-curtain and-threw herself upon Qamar al-Zamān, and-kissed-him in his-mouth like (the) beak-feeding (of) the-doves, and-embraced-him from (the) intensity (of) what-(was)-in-her of the-passion and-the-ardour.
sentences.i: She came out from behind the curtain, threw herself upon Qamar al-Zamān and kissed him on the mouth as doves feed one another beak to beak, and embraced him, so strong was the passion and longing in her.
sentences.n: ramā nafsahu ʿalā, “to throw oneself upon”. qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”; fī famihi, “on his mouth”. zaqq, verbal noun of zaqqa, “(of a bird) to feed its young from the beak”: doves billing. mā bihā mina …, “what was in her of …”: bi- marks where a feeling or ailment lodges, and min names it; the print runs mā and bihā together, مابها, and it is kept as set. wajd and gharām, two words for passionate love, rhyme with al-ḥamām. The print spells fī here with ي; the shaddas of وقبّلته, زقّ and شدّة are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي هَلْ هٰذَا يَقْظَةٌ أَمْ مَنَامٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī hal hādhā yaqẓatun am manāmun
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O my-lord, is this waking or dream?
sentences.i: And she said to him, “My lord, is this waking or a dream?”
sentences.n: hal … am …, “is it … or …?”, a question offering two choices. yaqẓa, “wakefulness”; manām, “sleep, a dream”, which rhymes with al-gharām just before.

sentences.t: وَهَلْ قَدْ مَنَّ اللّٰهُ عَلَيْنَا بِالْقُرْبِ بَعْدَ الْبِعَادِ فَالْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ عَلَى جَمْعِ شَمْلِنَا بَعْدَ الْيَأْسِ
sentences.tr: wa-hal qad manna Allāhu ʿalaynā bi-al-qurbi baʿda al-biʿādi fa-al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā jamʿi shamlinā baʿda al-yaʾsi
sentences.l: And-has indeed bestowed God upon-us the-nearness after the-distance? So-the-praise (is) to-God for (the) gathering (of) our-union after the-despair!
sentences.i: Has God truly granted us to be near after being far apart? Praise be to God for bringing us together after we had lost hope!
sentences.n: hal qad, “has … indeed?”: hal with qad is usual in later Arabic, though Classical grammar frowns on it. manna ʿalā … bi-, “to bestow … on someone as a favour”: ʿalā marks the one favoured and bi- the gift; its shadda is printed. qurb and biʿād, “nearness” and “distance”, a pair. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā, “praise be to God for”: li- marks the one praised, ʿalā the cause. jamʿ shamlinā, “the gathering of our union”, answering the tafarruq shamlinā of her verses. The hamza and sukūn of اليأْس are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا الْخَادِمُ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ ذَهَبَ يَجْرِي حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ فَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā al-khādimu ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati dhahaba yajrī ḥattā waṣala ilā al-maliki al-Ghayūri fa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And-when saw-her the-eunuch in that the-state, he-went running until he-reached to the-King al-Ghayūr, and-kissed the-ground between his-two-hands.
sentences.i: When the eunuch saw her in that state he ran off until he came to King al-Ghayūr, and kissed the ground before him
sentences.n: ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati, “in that state”: ʿalā marks the condition someone is in. dhahaba yajrī, “he went running”, the imperfect describing how he went. qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi, “he kissed the ground between his hands”, the courtly obeisance. The آ of رآها is printed; the shadda of فقبّل too.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا مَوْلَايَ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْمُنَجِّمَ شَيْخُ الْمُنَجِّمِينَ وَأَعْلَمُهُمْ كُلِّهِمْ فَإِنَّهُ دَاوَى ابْنَتَكَ وَهُوَ وَاقِفٌ خَلْفَ السِّتَارَةِ وَلَمْ يَدْخُلْ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā mawlāya iʿlam anna hādhā al-munajjima shaykhu al-munajjimīna wa-aʿlamuhum kullihim fa-innahu dāwā ibnataka wa-huwa wāqifun khalfa al-sitārati wa-lam yadkhul ʿalayhā
sentences.l: and-said to-him: O my-master, know that this the-astrologer (is the) elder (of) the-astrologers and-(the)-most-learned-of-them, all-of-them, for-indeed-he has-treated your-daughter while-he (was) standing behind the-curtain, and-did-not go-in to-her.
sentences.i: and said to him, “My lord, know that this astrologer is the master of all astrologers and the most learned of them all: he has cured your daughter while standing behind the curtain, without going in to her.”
sentences.n: iʿlam, “know!”, imperative of ʿalima, the usual way of opening a report to a king. shaykh, “elder, master”, of a craft. aʿlamuhum kullihim, “the most learned of them all”: kull agrees with -hum, in the genitive. dāwā, Form III, “to treat, cure”. wa-huwa wāqifun, “while he was standing”, a clause of state with wa-. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (a person)”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ انْظُرْ جَيِّدًا أَصَحِيحٌ هٰذَا الْخَبَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku unẓur jayyidan a-ṣaḥīḥun hādhā al-khabaru
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-king: Look well: (is it) true, this the-news?
sentences.i: The king said to him, “Look carefully: is this news true?”
sentences.n: unẓur, “look”, imperative of naẓara. jayyidan, “well”, an adjective in the accusative used as an adverb. a-ṣaḥīḥun hādhā al-khabaru, “is this news true?”: the question particle a- is prefixed to the fronted predicate.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَادِمُ يَاسَيِّدِي قُمْ وَانْظُرْ إِلَيْهَا كَيْفَ وَجَدَتْ فِيهَا قُوَّةً حَتَّى قَطَعَتِ السَّلَاسِلَ مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ وَخَرَجَتْ إِلَى الْمُنَجِّمِ تُقَبِّلُهُ وَتُعَانِقُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khādimu yā sayyidī qum wa-unẓur ilayhā kayfa wajadat fīhā quwwatan ḥattā qaṭaʿati al-salāsila mina al-ḥadīdi wa-kharajat ilā al-munajjimi tuqabbiluhu wa-tuʿāniquhu
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-eunuch: O my-lord, rise and-look at-her, how she-found in-herself strength until she-broke the-chains of iron and-came-out to the-astrologer, kissing-him and-embracing-him.
sentences.i: The eunuch said, “My lord, get up and look at her: see how she found the strength in herself to break the iron chains and come out to the astrologer, and is kissing and embracing him!”
sentences.n: The print runs yā and sayyidī together, ياسيدي; it is kept as set. naẓara ilā, “to look at”, ilā marking what is looked at. kayfa, “how”, brings in what he is to see. fīhā, “in her(self)”. mina al-ḥadīdi, “of iron”: min marks the material. tuqabbiluhu wa-tuʿāniquhu, two imperfects of state: “kissing him and embracing him”. The sukūn of وجدتْ is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ قَامَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى بِنْتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāma al-maliku al-Ghayūru wa-dakhala ʿalā bintihi
sentences.l: And-at that rose the-King al-Ghayūr and-went-in to his-daughter.
sentences.i: Thereupon King al-Ghayūr rose and went in to his daughter.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “thereupon”. bint, “daughter”, the everyday form beside ibna, used a little earlier.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ نَهَضَتْ قَائِمَةً وَغَطَّتْ رَأْسَهَا وَأَنْشَدَتْ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu nahaḍat qāʾimatan wa-ghaṭṭat raʾsahā wa-anshadat hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And-when she-saw-him, she-rose standing and-covered her-head and-recited these-two the-two-verses:
sentences.i: When she saw him she rose to her feet, covered her head, and recited these two verses:
sentences.n: nahaḍat qāʾimatan, “she rose, standing”, the participle of state in the accusative. ghaṭṭā, Form II, “to cover”: she veils her head before her father. hādhayni al-baytayni, “these two verses”, both dual in the accusative. The hamzas of رأته and رأسها, the ئ of قائمة and the shadda of وغطّت are printed.

sentences.t:
لَا اُحِبُّ السِّوَاكَ مِنْ اَجْلِ اَنِّيْ * اِنْ ذَكَرْتُ السِّوَاكَ قُلْتُ سِوَاكَا
وَاُحِبُّ الْاَرَاكَ مِنْ اَجْلِ اَنِّيْ * اِنْ ذَكَرْتُ الْاَرَاكَ قُلْتُ اَرَاكَا
sentences.tr:
lā uḥibbu al-siwāka min ajli annī * in dhakartu al-siwāka qultu siwākā
wa-uḥibbu al-arāka min ajli annī * in dhakartu al-arāka qultu arākā
sentences.l:
Not I-love the-tooth-stick, because that-I, * if I-mention the-tooth-stick, I-say “other-than-you”;
and-I-love the-arāk, because that-I, * if I-mention the-arāk, I-say “I-see-you”.
sentences.i:
I do not love the tooth-stick, siwāk, because * whenever I name it, I say “siwāka — other than you”;
but I love the arāk tree, because * whenever I name it, I say “arāka — I see you”.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. Both lines turn on a pun. siwāk is the twig used to clean the teeth; siwāka, said with a pronoun, is “other than you”, from siwā, “other than”, + -ka. arāk is the tree from whose twigs such sticks are cut; arāka is “I see you”, from raʾā, “to see”, + -ka. So she loves the tree whose name says “I see you” and not the stick whose name says “someone other than you”. The final -ā of siwākā and arākā is the lengthening of the rhyme. min ajli annī, “for the reason that I”, a causal phrase: min marks the cause. in dhakartu …, qultu …, “if I mention …, I say …”: both verbs perfect, as usual after in. The print sets a sukūn on the yāʾ of اَنِّيْ, as it often does on a long vowel.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ فَرِحَ أَبُوهَا بِسَلَامَتِهَا حَتَّى كَادَأَنْ يَطِيرَ وَقَبَّلَهَا بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهَا لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ يُحِبُّهَا مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika fariḥa abūhā bi-salāmatihā ḥattā kāda an yaṭīra wa-qabbalahā bayna ʿaynayhā li-annahu kāna yuḥibbuhā maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: And-at that rejoiced her-father at-her-soundness, until he-was-about to fly; and-he-kissed-her between her-two-eyes, because-he was loving-her (with) a-love great.
sentences.i: At that her father was so glad to see her well again that he almost flew for joy; and he kissed her between the eyes, for he loved her very dearly.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause of the joy. salāma, “soundness, safety”, here her recovery. kāda an yaṭīra, “he nearly flew”: kāda, “to be on the point of”, here with an and the subjunctive; the print runs kāda and an together, كادان, and it is kept as set. li-annahu, “because he”: li-, “for”, with anna. yuḥibbuhā maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan, “he loved her with a great love”, the verbal noun as an inner object. The shaddas of وقبّلها, يحبّها and محبّة are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ مِنْ أَيِّ الْبِلَادِ أَنْتَ
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala al-maliku al-Ghayūru ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-saʾalahu ʿan ḥālihi wa-qāla lahu min ayyi al-bilādi anta
sentences.l: And-turned the-King al-Ghayūr to Qamar al-Zamān and-asked-him about his-state, and-said to-him: From which (of) the-lands (are) you?
sentences.i: Then King al-Ghayūr turned to Qamar al-Zamān, asked him how he did, and said to him, “What country are you from?”
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, Form IV, “to turn towards, give one's attention to”. saʾala … ʿan, “to ask … about”: the hamza of وسأله is printed. min ayyi al-bilādi, “from which of the lands”; the shadda of ايّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِنَسَبِهِ وَشَأْنِهِ وَأَعْلَمَهُ أَنَّ وَالِدَهُ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarahu Qamaru al-Zamāni bi-nasabihi wa-shaʾnihi wa-aʿlamahu anna wālidahu al-maliku Shahramānu
sentences.l: And-informed-him Qamar al-Zamān of-his-lineage and-his-affair, and-made-him-know that his-father (was) the-King Shahramān.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān told him his lineage and his circumstances, and let him know that his father was King Shahramān.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, Form IV, “to inform someone of”: the verb takes bi- for the news. nasab, “lineage”; shaʾn, “affair, standing”, which the print writes without its hamza, شانه. aʿlama, Form IV of ʿalima, “to make know, inform”. anna wālidahu al-maliku Shahramānu: after anna the subject is accusative, wālidahu, and the predicate nominative.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَصَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقِصَّةَ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا إِلَى آخِرِهَا وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِجَمِيعِ مَا اتَّفَقَ لَهُ مَعَ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَكَيْفَ أَخَذَ الْخَاتَمَ مِنْ إِصْبَعِهَا وَأَلْبَسَهَا خَاتَمَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni qaṣṣa ʿalayhi al-qiṣṣata min awwalihā ilā ākhirihā wa-akhbarahu bi-jamīʿi mā ittafaqa lahu maʿa al-sitti Budūra wa-kayfa akhadha al-khātama min iṣbaʿihā wa-albasahā khātamahu
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān related to-him the-story from its-beginning to its-end, and-informed-him of-all what happened to-him with the-Lady Budūr, and-how he-took the-ring from her-finger and-made-her-wear his-ring.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān told him the story from beginning to end, and told him all that had passed between him and the Lady Budūr, and how he had taken the ring from her finger and put his own ring on her.
sentences.n: thumma inna …, “then …”: inna only opens the new step of the story. qaṣṣa ʿalā, “to relate to”, ʿalā marking the hearer; its shadda is printed. ittafaqa li-, Form VIII, “to happen to”, li- marking the one it befalls. albasa, Form IV of labisa, “to clothe, put (a ring) on someone”, with two objects. iṣbaʿ, “finger”. The آ of آخرها is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِنَّ حِكَايَتَكُمَا يَنْبَغِي أَنْ تُؤَرَّخَ فِى الْكُتُبِ وَتُقْرَأَ بَعْدَ كُمَا جِيلًا بَعْدَ جِيلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-maliku al-Ghayūru min dhālika wa-qāla lahu inna ḥikāyatakumā yanbaghī an tuʾarrakha fī al-kutubi wa-tuqraʾa baʿdakumā jīlan baʿda jīlin
sentences.l: And-wondered the-King al-Ghayūr at that, and-said to-him: Indeed your-two's-tale, it-is-fitting that it-be-chronicled in the-books and-be-read after-you-two, generation after generation.
sentences.i: King al-Ghayūr marvelled at it and said to him, “The tale of you two ought to be set down in the chronicles and read after you, generation after generation.”
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to wonder at”: min marks what causes the wonder. -kumā, “you two”, the dual pronoun. yanbaghī an, “it is fitting that”. tuʾarrakha, passive of arrakha, Form II, “to date, record in a chronicle”; tuqraʾa, passive of qaraʾa, “to read”: both subjunctive after an; the ؤ of تؤرخ and the hamza of وتقرأ are printed. The print splits baʿdakumā, “after you two”, into بعد كما; it is kept as set. jīlan baʿda jīlin, “generation after generation”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ الْغَيُورَ أَحْضَرَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ الْقُضَاةَ وَالشُّهُودَ وَكَتَبَ كِتَابَ السَّيِّدَةِ بُدُورَ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَأَمَرَ بِتَزْيِينِ الْمَدِينَةِ سَبْعَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika al-Ghayūra aḥḍara min waqtihi al-quḍāta wa-al-shuhūda wa-kataba kitāba al-sayyidati Budūra ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-amara bi-tazyīni al-madīnati sabʿata ayyāmin
sentences.l: Then indeed the-King al-Ghayūr summoned from his-time the-judges and-the-witnesses, and-wrote (the) contract (of) the-Lady Budūr upon Qamar al-Zamān, and-ordered the-adorning (of) the-city (for) seven days.
sentences.i: Then King al-Ghayūr at once summoned the judges and witnesses and had the contract drawn up marrying the Lady Budūr to Qamar al-Zamān, and gave orders for the city to be decorated for seven days.
sentences.n: aḥḍara, Form IV, “to bring, summon”. quḍāt, plural of qāḍī, “judge”; shuhūd, plural of shāhid, “witness”: the two needed for a marriage contract. kataba kitābahā ʿalā, “to write her contract upon”, the set phrase for marrying a woman to a man; ʿalā marks the husband. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded. tazyīn, Form II verbal noun, “adorning, decking out” with lamps and hangings for a festival.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَدُّوا السِّمَاطَ وَالْأَطْعِمَةَ وَعُمِلَتِ الْأَفْرَاحُ وَتَزَيَّنَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ وَجَمِيعُ الْعَسَاكِرِ بِأَفْخَرِ الثِّيَابِ وَأَقْبَلَتِ الْبَشَائِرُ وَدُقَّتِ الطُّبُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma maddū al-simāṭa wa-al-aṭʿimata wa-ʿumilati al-afrāḥu wa-tazayyanati al-madīnatu wa-jamīʿu al-ʿasākiri bi-afkhari al-thiyābi wa-aqbalati al-bashāʾiru wa-duqqati al-ṭubūlu
sentences.l: Then they-spread the-cloth and-the-foods, and-were-made the-rejoicings, and-adorned-itself the-city and-all the-troops with-(the)-finest (of) the-clothes, and-came the-good-tidings, and-were-beaten the-drums.
sentences.i: Then they spread the banquet-cloth and the dishes, the festivities were held, the city and all the troops put on their finest clothes, the glad tidings came pouring in, and the drums were beaten.
sentences.n: maddū, “they spread”, from madda, “to stretch out”; the subject is the king's people, unnamed. simāṭ, the long cloth laid on the floor for a feast. ʿumilati al-afrāḥu, “the rejoicings were made”, passive of ʿamila; afrāḥ, plural of faraḥ, in later Arabic “wedding festivities”. tazayyana bi-, Form V, “to adorn oneself with”: bi- marks the finery. bashāʾir, plural of bishāra, “good news”, and the gifts and heralds that bring it; its ئ is printed. duqqat, passive of daqqa, “to beat (a drum)”. The shaddas of وتزيّنت and ودقّت are printed.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَفَرِحَ أَبُوهَا بِعَافِيَتِهَا وَزَوَاجِهَا وَحَمِدَ اللّٰهَ الَّذِي رَمَاهَا فِي حُبِّ شَابٍّ مَلِيحٍ مِنْ أَبْنَاءِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhala Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā al-sitti Budūra wa-fariḥa abūhā bi-ʿāfiyatihā wa-zawājihā wa-ḥamida Allāha alladhī ramāhā fī ḥubbi shābbin malīḥin min abnāʾi al-mulūki
sentences.l: And-went-in Qamar al-Zamān to the-Lady Budūr; and-rejoiced her-father at-her-health and-her-marriage, and-praised God who cast-her into (the) love (of) a-youth handsome from (the) sons (of) the-kings.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān went in to the Lady Budūr; and her father rejoiced at her recovery and her marriage, and praised God who had made her fall in love with a handsome young man, a son of kings.
sentences.n: The print has بعانيتها, a misprint for بعافيتها, corrected here. dakhala ʿalā, of a bridegroom, “to go in to (his bride)”: the consummation of the marriage. fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause, here ʿāfiya, “health, recovery”, and zawāj, “marriage”. ramāhā fī, “cast her into”: love is a pit one falls into. malīḥ, “handsome, comely”. abnāʾ, plural of ibn, “son”.

sentences.t: فَجَلَوْهَا عَلَيْهِ وَكَانَا يُشْبِهَانِ بَعْضَهُمَا فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ وَالظَّرْفِ وَالدَّلَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalawhā ʿalayhi wa-kānā yushbihāni baʿḍahumā fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli wa-al-ẓarfi wa-al-dalāli
sentences.l: And-they-displayed-her to-him, and-they-two-were resembling each-other in the-beauty and-the-loveliness and-the-grace and-the-coquetry.
sentences.i: They displayed her to him in her bridal finery, and the two were like each other in beauty and loveliness, in grace and charm.
sentences.n: jalā al-ʿarūsa ʿalā, “to display the bride to (her husband)”, the unveiling of the bride in her successive dresses; ʿalā marks the one she is shown to. kānā yushbihāni, “the two were resembling”, dual, kāna with the imperfect for an ongoing state. ashbaha, Form IV, “to resemble”; baʿḍahumā, “each other”, literally “some of the two”, the later way of saying it, where Classical prose has baʿḍuhumā baʿḍan. ḥusn and jamāl, two words for beauty; ẓarf, “elegance, wit”; dalāl, “coquetry, playful airs”. The list rhymes, al-jamāl / al-dalāl.

sentences.t: فَنَامَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عِنْدَهَا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَبَلَغَ أَرَبَهُ مِنْهَا وَهِيَ بَلَّتْ شَوْتَهَا مِنْهُ وَتَمَتَّعَتْ بِحُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ وَتَعَانَقَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-nāma Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿindahā tilka al-laylata wa-balagha arabahu minhā wa-hiya ballat shawtahā minhu wa-tamattaʿat bi-ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi wa-taʿānaqā ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-slept Qamar al-Zamān with-her that the-night, and-reached his-desire of-her; and-she quenched her-desire(?) of-him, and-enjoyed his-beauty and-his-loveliness, and-they-two-embraced until the-morning.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān slept with her that night and had his desire of her, and she quenched her desire for him and took her pleasure of his beauty and loveliness, and they lay in each other's arms until morning.
sentences.n: tilka al-laylata, “that night”, accusative of time. balagha arabahu min, “to attain one's desire of”, said of the act of love; arab, “need, desire”; min marks the one it is had from. ballat, “she moistened, quenched”, from balla, its shadda printed, the phrase made on balla ghalīlahu, “to quench one's burning thirst”. The next word is doubtful: the print has شوتها, which is no word as it stands; it is probably shahwatahā, “her desire”, with the hāʾ dropped, or shawqahā, “her longing”. The print is kept and read here as “her desire”; the pointing shawtahā only follows the letters. tamattaʿa bi-, Form V, “to enjoy”: bi- marks what is enjoyed; its shadda is printed. taʿānaqā, Form VI dual, “they embraced each other”.

sentences.t: وَفِى الْيَوْمِ الثَّانِي عَمِلَ الْمَلِكُ وَلِيمَةً وَجَمَعَ فِيهَا جَمِيعَ أَهْلِ الْجَزَائِرِ الْجَوَّانِيَّهْ وَالْبَرَّانِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī al-yawmi al-thānī ʿamila al-maliku walīmatan wa-jamaʿa fīhā jamīʿa ahli al-jazāʾiri al-jawwāniyya wa-al-barrāniyyati
sentences.l: And-on the-day the-second the-king made a-banquet and-gathered at-it all (the) people (of) the-Islands the-inner and-the-outer.
sentences.i: On the next day the king gave a wedding feast and gathered at it all the people of the Inner and Outer Islands,
sentences.n: walīma, “banquet”, especially a wedding feast. al-Jazāʾir, “the Islands”, King al-Ghayūr's realm; al-jawwāniyya and al-barrāniyya, “the inner” and “the outer”, colloquial adjectives from jawwā, “inside”, and barrā, “outside”. The print spells the first with ه for ة, الجوانيه, as it often does; it is read al-jawwāniyya. The ئ of الجزائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمَ لَهُمُ الْأَسْمِطَةَ وَالطَّعَامَ الْفَاخِرَ وَامْتَدَّتِ الْمَوَائِدُ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qaddama lahumu al-asmiṭata wa-al-ṭaʿāma al-fākhira wa-imtaddati al-mawāʾidu muddata shahrin kāmilin
sentences.l: and-set-before them the-cloths and-the-food the-splendid, and-were-spread the-tables (for a) space (of) a-month complete.
sentences.i: and set before them the laden cloths and splendid food, and the tables stayed spread for a whole month.
sentences.n: qaddama li-, Form II, “to set before, offer to”: li- marks the guests; its shadda is printed. asmiṭa, plural of simāṭ, the feast-cloth. imtadda, Form VIII of madda, “to be stretched out, extend”. mawāʾid, plural of māʾida, “table (of food)”; its ئ is printed. muddata shahrin kāmilin, “for the space of a whole month”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ أَنِ اسْتَهْدَى سِرُّ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَبَلَغَ أَرَبَهُ وَمَكَثَ فِي هٰذَا الْحَالِ مَعَ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ مُدَّةً تَفَكَّرَ وَالِدَهُ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda ani istahdā sirru Qamari al-Zamāni wa-balagha arabahu wa-makatha fī hādhā al-ḥāli maʿa al-sitti Budūra muddatan tafakkara wālidahu al-malika Shahramāna
sentences.l: And-after that grew-calm(?) (the) heart (of) Qamar al-Zamān and-he-reached his-desire and-stayed in this the-state with the-Lady Budūr a-while, he-remembered his-father the-King Shahramān.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān's heart was at rest and he had his desire, and he had lived so with the Lady Budūr for a while, he remembered his father, King Shahramān.
sentences.n: The first verb is doubtful. As printed, istahdā is Form X of hadā, “to ask for guidance”, which does not suit sirr, “the inmost heart”, as its subject. It is most likely for istahdaʾa, from hadaʾa, “to grow calm”, its final hamza written as ى, a common later spelling: “after Qamar al-Zamān's heart had grown calm”. The print is kept and read in that sense; its shadda on سرّ is printed. baʿda an, “after”, with the perfect; an takes a helping kasra before the next word. makatha, “to stay”; al-ḥāl, “the state”, here masculine with hādhā. muddatan, “for a while”. tafakkara, Form V, “to reflect”, in later Arabic also “to remember”, and here, as in speech, it takes its object directly, without fī.

sentences.t: فَرَآهُ فِى الْمَنَامِ وَهُوَ يَقُولُ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي أَهٰكَذَا تَفْعَلُ مَعِي هٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾāhu fī al-manāmi wa-huwa yaqūlu lahu yā waladī a-hākadhā tafʿalu maʿī hādhihi al-fiʿāla
sentences.l: And-he-saw-him in the-dream, and-he (was) saying to-him: O my-son, is-it-thus you-do with-me these the-deeds?
sentences.i: And he saw him in a dream, saying to him, “My son, is this how you treat me?”
sentences.n: wa-huwa yaqūlu, “while he was saying”, a clause of state. a-hākadhā, “is it thus?”: the question particle a- on hākadhā, “thus, like this”. faʿala maʿa, “to do to, treat”, maʿa marking the one treated. fiʿāl, “deeds”, plural of fiʿl, here with the reproach of “such conduct”. The آ of فرآه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدَهُ فِى النَّوْمِ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadahu fī al-nawmi hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And-he-recited-to-him in the-sleep these-two the-two-verses:
sentences.i: And in the dream he recited to him these two verses:
sentences.n: anshadahu, “he recited to him”: anshada, Form IV, takes the hearer as a direct object, and the verses as a second. nawm, “sleep”.

sentences.t:
لَقَدْ رَاعَنِي بَدْرُ الدُّجَى بِصُدُودِهِ * وَوَكَّلَ اَجْفَانِي بِرَعْيِ كَوَاكِبِهْ
فَيَاكَبِدِي مَهْلًا عَسَاهُ يَعُودُ لِي * وَيَا مُهْجَتِي صَبْرًا عَلَى مَاكَوَاكَ بِهِ
sentences.tr:
laqad rāʿanī badru al-dujā bi-ṣudūdihi * wa-wakkala ajfānī bi-raʿyi kawākibih
fa-yā kabidī mahlan ʿasāhu yaʿūdu lī * wa-yā muhjatī ṣabran ʿalā mā kawāka bihi
sentences.l:
Indeed alarmed-me (the) full-moon (of) the-darkness by-his-turning-away, * and-set my-eyelids to-watching his-stars.
So-O my-liver, gently! Perhaps-he will-return to-me; * and-O my-heart's-blood, patience over what he-branded-you with-it!
sentences.i:
The full moon of the night has dismayed me by turning away, * and set my eyes to keep watch over his stars.
Gently, my liver! Perhaps he will come back to me; * and patience, my heart, under the brand he has burned on you.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on kawākibih / bihi. rāʿa, “to frighten, dismay”. badr al-dujā, “the full moon of the darkness”, the beloved, here the son: badr is also the singular behind the name Budūr. ṣudūd, “turning away, avoidance”: bi- marks the means. wakkala … bi-, Form II, “to charge someone with (a task)”: bi- marks the task, raʿy, “watching, tending”, as a sleepless lover counts the stars; kawākibih, with the -hi of the rhyme pronounced short in pause. kabid, “liver”, and muhja, “heart's blood, soul”, are both seats of feeling. mahlan, “gently, slowly!”, and ṣabran, “patience!”, accusatives standing for a command. ʿasāhu, “perhaps he”. The print runs yā and kabidī together, فَيَاكَبِدِي, and mā and kawāka, مَاكَوَاكَ; both are kept as set. kawā, “to brand, cauterise”: ʿalā mā kawāka bihi, “over what he has branded you with”, bi- marking the brand.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا رَأَى وَالِدَهُ فِى الْمَنَامِ وَهُوَ يُعَاتِبُهُ أَصْبَحَ مَغْمُومًا حَزِينًا
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā raʾā wālidahu fī al-manāmi wa-huwa yuʿātibuhu aṣbaḥa maghmūman ḥazīnan
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān, when he-saw his-father in the-dream while-he (was) reproaching-him, he-became-in-the-morning grieved, sad.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān had seen his father in a dream reproaching him, he woke in the morning troubled and sad.
sentences.n: ʿātaba, Form III, “to reproach (a friend), chide”. aṣbaḥa, “to be in the morning”, and so “to become”, with its predicate in the accusative. maghmūm, “grieved, oppressed with care”, passive participle of ghamma. The hamza of رأى is printed.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَتْهُ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ فَأَخْبَرَهَا بِمَا رَآهُ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾalathu al-sittu Budūru fa-akhbarahā bi-mā raʾāhu
sentences.l: And-asked-him the-Lady Budūr, and-he-informed-her of-what he-saw-it.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr asked him what was wrong, and he told her what he had seen.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, “to inform someone of”: the verb takes bi- for the news, here bi-mā, “of what”. raʾāhu, “he saw it”, the -hu returning to mā. The hamza of فسألته and the آ of رآه are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print splits the name here, شهر زاد; it is kept as set.
